claim: An S3 Bucket Key for SSE-KMS can reduce AWS KMS request costs by up to 99 percent by decreasing the request traffic from S3 to KMS.
question: By how much can S3 Bucket Keys reduce the KMS request cost of SSE-KMS?

qualifiers.condition: savings depend on the number of requesters, request patterns and object age

evidence.quote: Using a bucket-level key for SSE-KMS can reduce AWS KMS request costs by up to 99 percent by decreasing the request traffic from Amazon S3 to AWS KMS.

claim: With an S3 Bucket Key enabled, KMS CloudTrail events log the bucket ARN instead of the object ARN, and there are fewer KMS CloudTrail events for SSE-KMS objects.
question: What changes in CloudTrail when S3 Bucket Keys are enabled?

values.display: log your bucket ARN instead of your object ARN

qualifiers.scope: per bucket using SSE-KMS with a Bucket Key

evidence.quote: After you enable an S3 Bucket Key, your AWS KMS CloudTrail events log your bucket ARN instead of your object ARN. Additionally, you see fewer KMS CloudTrail events for SSE-KMS objects in your logs.

claim: Starting April 2026, SSE-C is disabled by default for all new general purpose buckets and for existing buckets in accounts with no SSE-C encrypted objects; to use it you set BlockedEncryptionTypes to NONE with PutBucketEncryption.
question: Is SSE-C allowed by default on a new S3 bucket?

qualifiers.scope: new general purpose buckets, and existing buckets in accounts with no SSE-C encrypted objects
qualifiers.condition: while blocked, writes that specify SSE-C fail with HTTP 403 AccessDenied

evidence.quote: Starting April 2026, SSE-C is disabled by default for all new general purpose buckets and existing buckets in accounts with no SSE-C encrypted objects.
If your workload requires SSE-C, you must explicitly enable it by setting `BlockedEncryptionTypes` to `NONE` in your bucket's default encryption configuration using the `PutBucketEncryption` API.

note: d043; FRESHNESS item 'SSE-C disabled by default'. GA April 2026, before 2026-07-15, so examinable by the book's rule, but older questions assume SSE-C works on any bucket. The old default is not stated verbatim, so no 'changed' value is recorded.

claim: With SSE-C, S3 never stores the encryption key, so you must supply it every time the data is downloaded, and requests with SSE-C headers must use HTTPS.
question: Does S3 store the SSE-C key, and must SSE-C requests use HTTPS?

values.display: S3 never stores the encryption key

evidence.quote: S3 never stores the encryption key when you use SSE-C. You must supply the encryption key every time you want anyone to download your SSE-C encrypted data from S3.
You must use HTTPS when specifying SSE-C headers on your requests.
